items.text: Impeller Reynolds Number

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| ρ | Fluid density | kg/m³ |
| N | Impeller rotational speed | rev/s |
| D | Impeller diameter | m |
| μ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |

**Regime classification:** Re < 10 laminar; 10 < Re < 10,000 transitional; Re > 10,000 turbulent.

**Reference:** Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 6.
Power Number & Impeller Power

N<sub>p</sub> is the **power number**, a dimensionless constant that depends on impeller geometry and Re.

| Impeller Type | N<sub>p</sub> (turbulent) |
|---------------|-------------------|
| Rushton turbine (6-blade) | 5.0 |
| Pitched-blade turbine (45°, 4-blade) | 1.27 |
| Retreat-curve impeller | 0.3 – 0.5 |
| A310 / A320 hydrofoil | 0.3 |
| Magnetic stir bar | 0.3 – 0.5 (approx.) |

For laminar flow: N<sub>p</sub> ≈ 70 / Re.

**Reference:** Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 6.
Power per Unit Volume (Specific Energy Dissipation)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| P | Impeller power draw | W |
| V | Liquid volume | m³ |
| ε | Mean specific energy dissipation rate | W/m³ |

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Impeller Tip Speed

Tip speed is a common scale-up criterion and relates to shear at the impeller.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Pumping Rate

N<sub>Q</sub> is the **pumping number** (flow number).  Typical values:

| Impeller | N<sub>Q</sub> |
|----------|-------|
| Rushton turbine | 0.72 |
| Pitched-blade turbine (down-pumping) | 0.79 |
| A310 hydrofoil | 0.56 |

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Kolmogorov Length Scale

The smallest eddy size in turbulent flow.  Below this scale, viscous dissipation dominates.
Typical values: 10 – 100 µm in stirred tanks.

**Important:** ε here is the **mass-specific** energy dissipation rate in **W/kg** (= m²/s³),
i.e. ε = P / (ρV), not P/V in W/m³.

**Reference:** Kolmogorov, A.N. (1991). The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers. [*Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A*](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075), 434, 9–13. (English translation of the 1941 *Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR*, 30, 301–305.)
Maximum Local Energy Dissipation Rate

The energy dissipation rate near the impeller can be 1–2 orders of magnitude
higher than the mean. 

**Reference:** Grenville, Richard & Giacomelli, Jason & Brown, David & Padron, Gustavo. (2017). Mixing: Impeller performance in stirred tanks. [*Chemical Engineering*](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319042061_Mixing_Impeller_performance_in_stirred_tanks). 124. 42.
Average Shear Rate (Camp–Stein)
Derived from equating the volume-averaged viscous dissipation to the power input:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| P | Power input | W |
| μ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |
| V | Liquid volume | m³ |
| γ·<sub>avg</sub> | RMS average shear rate | 1/s |
**Reference:** Camp, T.R. & Stein, P.C. (1943). Velocity gradients and internal work in fluid motion. *J. Boston Soc. Civil Eng.*, 30, 219–237.
Maximum Shear Rate (Impeller Zone)

Evaluated using ε<sub>max</sub> from the Maximum Local Energy Dissipation Rate equation above.  This gives the peak
shear rate in the impeller discharge zone.

**Reference:** standard turbulence dissipation relation ε = ν γ̇² (e.g. Tennekes, H. & Lumley, J.L. (1972). *A First Course in Turbulence*, MIT Press, Ch. 3); ε<sub>max</sub> estimate from Kresta & Wood (1993), as above.
Shear Stress

For Newtonian fluids, shear stress (Pa) is simply viscosity multiplied by
the shear rate.  Both τ<sub>avg</sub> and τ<sub>max</sub> are reported.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Circulation Time

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| V | Liquid volume | m³ |
| N<sub>q</sub> | Pumping (flow) number | — |
| N | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| D | Impeller diameter | m |

The mean time for a fluid element to complete one loop through the
impeller zone.  Related to blend time via θ<sub>95</sub> ≈ 5.2  t<sub>c</sub>.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 9.
Impeller Torque

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| P | Impeller power draw | W |
| N | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| Λ | Torque | N·m |

**Torque per unit volume** (Λ)/(V) provides a scale-independent measure
of mechanical stress on the fluid.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Energy Dissipation Circulation Function (EDCF)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| ε<sub>max</sub> | Maximum local energy dissipation rate | W/kg |
| t<sub>c</sub> | Circulation time | s |
| EDCF | Mixing intensity × exposure frequency | W/kg/s |

EDCF combines the **intensity** of the impeller discharge zone with the
**frequency** at which fluid passes through it.

**Reference:** Nienow, A.W. (1997). On impeller circulation and mixing effectiveness in the turbulent flow regime. [*Chem. Eng. Sci.*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0009-2509%2897%2900072-9), 52(15), 2557–2565.
Froude Number

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| N | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| D | Impeller diameter | m |
| g | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |

Ratio of inertial to gravitational forces.  Important for predicting
free-surface vortex formation in unbaffled or partially baffled vessels.

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 6.
Macro-Blend Time (95 %)

This represents the time to achieve 95 % uniformity on the bulk (macro) scale.

**Reference**: [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 9.
Engulfment Micromixing Time

Baldyga & Bourne engulfment model – characterises the time for mixing at the
smallest (molecular) scales.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| ν | Kinematic viscosity (μ / ρ) | m²/s |
| ε | Mass-specific energy dissipation rate P/(ρ V) | W/kg (= m²/s³) |

**Reference:** Baldyga, J. & Bourne, J.R. (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710), Wiley.
Damköhler Numbers
Macro Damköhler Number
Micro Damköhler Number

| Da range | Interpretation |
|-----------|----------------|
| Da ≪ 0.01 | Reaction-limited – insensitive to mixing |
| 0.01 < Da < 0.1 | Likely insensitive |
| 0.1 < Da < 1 | Potentially sensitive |
| 1 < Da < 10 | Mixing-sensitive |
| Da ≫ 10 | Strongly mixing-limited |

**Reference:** Paul, E.L., Atiemo-Obeng, V.A. & Kresta, S.M. (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Wiley, Ch. 13.
Gas-Liquid Damköhler Number

Compares the characteristic **gas-liquid mass-transfer time** (1/k<sub>L</sub> a) to
the reaction time.

| Da<sub>GL</sub> range | Interpretation |
|----------------|----------------|
| Da<sub>GL</sub> ≪ 0.01 | Mass transfer is fast — reaction-limited |
| 0.01 < Da<sub>GL</sub> < 0.1 | Likely insensitive to G-L transfer |
| 0.1 < Da<sub>GL</sub> < 1 | Potentially transfer-limited |
| 1 < Da<sub>GL</sub> < 10 | Transfer-limited |
| Da<sub>GL</sub> ≫ 10 | Strongly transfer-limited |

When k<sub>L</sub> a = 0 (no gas phase present), Da<sub>GL</sub> is set to zero (not applicable).

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 13.
Solid-Liquid Damköhler Number

Compares the characteristic **solid-liquid mass-transfer time** (1/k<sub>L</sub> a<sub>SL</sub>)
to the reaction time, where k<sub>L</sub> a<sub>SL</sub> is the volumetric solid-liquid
mass-transfer coefficient:

k<sub>L</sub> a<sub>SL</sub> = k<sub>SL</sub> · a<sub>s</sub>,  a<sub>s</sub> = (6φ<sub>s</sub>)/(d<sub>p</sub>)

The slip velocity used in the Ranz-Marshall correlation is the larger of the
terminal settling velocity and the Kolmogorov-scale turbulent slip velocity:

v<sub>slip</sub> = max(v<sub>t</sub>, (ε · d<sub>p</sub>)<sup>1/3</sup>)

| Da<sub>SL</sub> range | Interpretation |
|----------------|----------------|
| Da<sub>SL</sub> ≪ 0.01 | Mass transfer is fast — reaction-limited |
| 0.01 < Da<sub>SL</sub> < 0.1 | Likely insensitive to S-L transfer |
| 0.1 < Da<sub>SL</sub> < 1 | Potentially transfer-limited |
| 1 < Da<sub>SL</sub> < 10 | Transfer-limited |
| Da<sub>SL</sub> ≫ 10 | Strongly transfer-limited |

When k<sub>L</sub> a<sub>SL</sub> = 0 (no solid phase present), Da<sub>SL</sub> is set to zero.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| k<sub>SL</sub> | Solid-liquid mass-transfer coefficient | m/s |
| a<sub>s</sub> | Specific particle surface area | 1/m |
| φ<sub>s</sub> | Volumetric solids fraction | — |
| d<sub>p</sub> | Particle diameter | m |
| v<sub>t</sub> | Terminal settling velocity | m/s |
| ε | Specific energy dissipation rate | W/kg |
| t<sub>rxn</sub> | Characteristic reaction time | s |

**Reference:** Paul *et al.* (2004). [*Handbook of Industrial Mixing*](https://doi.org/10.1002/0471451452), Ch. 13; Ranz, W.E. & Marshall, W.R. (1952). *Chem. Eng. Prog.*, 48, 141–146.
Characteristic Reaction Time
First-order or pseudo-first-order
Second-order

The characteristic reaction time is taken as the **reaction time constant**
(the e-folding time, i.e. the time for the limiting reagent to fall to 1/e of
its initial value), consistent with the Damköhler-number definition
Da = t<sub>mix</sub> / t<sub>rxn</sub>.  Note this is **not** the 50 % half-life
t<sub>1/2</sub> = ln 2 / k, which is ~30 % shorter for a first-order reaction.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| k | Rate constant | 1/s (1st order) or L/(mol·s) (2nd order) |
| C<sub>0</sub> | Initial concentration | mol/L |

**Reference:** Levenspiel, O. (1999). [*Chemical Reaction Engineering*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780471254249), 3rd ed. Wiley, Ch. 3.
Local Micromixing Time (Impeller Zone)

Same Baldyga & Bourne engulfment model, but evaluated using the **local maximum**
energy dissipation rate ε<sub>max</sub> near the impeller.  Relevant when
reagents are **fed directly into the impeller discharge zone**.

**Reference:** Baldyga, J. & Bourne, J.R. (1999). [*Turbulent Mixing and Chemical Reactions*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471981710), Wiley.
Mesomixing Time Scales

Mesomixing acts at the scale of the feed plume / feed-pipe diameter and has
**two** characteristic time scales (Baldyga & Bourne, 1999; Myerson 2019, Table 8.1).
Mixing Lab implements the inertial-convective (disintegration) scale below.
Inertial-Convective Disintegration

Break-up of the feed plume by inertial-convective disintegration of the large
eddies. Λ<sub>C</sub> is the integral scale of the velocity fluctuations, set by
the feed-pipe / plume size. **Mixing Lab implements this scale** using the
feed-pipe diameter d<sub>feed</sub> as the length scale with A = 1.2:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Λ<sub>C</sub> | Integral scale of velocity fluctuations | m |
| d<sub>feed</sub> | Feed-pipe internal diameter | m |
| ε | Local energy dissipation at the feed point | W/kg (= m²/s³) |
kLa – Volumetric Mass-Transfer Coefficient (Gas-Liquid)

Van 't Riet (1979) correlation for aerated stirred tanks.

| System | C<sub>1</sub> | C<sub>2</sub> | C<sub>3</sub> |
|--------|-------|-------|-------|
| Coalescing (pure liquids) | 0.026 | 0.4 | 0.5 |
| Non-coalescing (electrolytes) | 0.002 | 0.7 | 0.2 |

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| P/V | Gassed specific power input | W/m³ |
| v<sub>s</sub> | Superficial gas velocity | m/s |
| k<sub>L</sub> a | Volumetric mass-transfer coefficient | 1/s |

**Note:** v<sub>s</sub> = 0 (no sparging) → k<sub>L</sub> a = 0.

**Reference:** van 't Riet, K. (1979). Review of measuring methods and results in non-viscous gas-liquid mass transfer in stirred vessels. [*Ind. Eng. Chem. Process Des. Dev.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/i260071a001), 18(3), 357–364.
kLa – Free-Surface (Headspace) Mass Transfer

Lamont & Scott (1970) small-eddy surface-renewal model.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| D<sub>mol</sub> | Molecular diffusivity of dissolved gas | m²/s |
| ε | Mean specific energy dissipation rate | W/kg (= m²/s³) |
| ν | Kinematic viscosity | m²/s |
| D<sub>T</sub> | Tank inside diameter | m |
| V | Liquid volume | m³ |
| a<sub>surface</sub> | Specific interfacial area (free surface) | 1/m |

**Typical D<sub>mol</sub> values for common gases in water at 25 °C:**

| Gas | D<sub>mol</sub> (m²/s) |
|-----|------------------|
| O₂  | 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ |
| CO₂ | 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ |
| N₂  | 1.9 × 10⁻⁹ |
| H₂  | 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ |

**Reference:** Lamont, J.C. & Scott, D.S. (1970). An eddy cell model of mass transfer into the surface of a turbulent liquid. [*AIChE J.*](https://doi.org/10.1002/aic.690160403), 16(4), 513–519.
Miscibility Screening

**Two-tier approach:**

**1. Known-pair lookup** — Experimental miscibility data from standard references
(Perry's, CRC Handbook, Merck Index).

**2. Hansen Solubility Parameters (fallback):**

| R<sub>a</sub> (MPa<sup>0.5</sup>) | Interpretation |
|----------------------|----------------|
| < 15 | Likely **miscible** |
| 15 – 25 | Partially miscible / borderline |
| > 25 | Likely **immiscible** |

**Reference:** Hansen, C.M. (2007). [*Hansen Solubility Parameters: A User's Handbook*](https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420006834), 2nd ed. CRC Press.
Reaction Rate (Molar)
First-order or pseudo-first-order
Second-order or pseudo-second-order

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| k | Rate constant | 1/s (1st) or L/(mol·s) (2nd) |
| C<sub>0</sub> | Initial concentration | mol/L |
| V<sub>L</sub> | Liquid volume | L |

**Reference:** Levenspiel, O. (1999). [*Chemical Reaction Engineering*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780471254249), 3rd ed. Wiley.
Heat Generation Rate

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Δ H<sub>rxn</sub> | Enthalpy of reaction (negative = exothermic) | kJ/mol |
| r<sub>total</sub> | Total molar reaction rate | mol/s |
| Q<sub>gen</sub> | Rate of heat release | W |

**Reference:** Levenspiel (1999), Ch. 9.
Adiabatic Temperature Rise

The temperature the batch would reach if **all** reaction heat were retained
(no cooling).  Unlike the molar enthalpy alone, Δ T<sub>ad</sub> accounts for
reagent concentration and the thermal mass of the mixture, and is the basis of
the Stoessel criticality classification used to rank thermal-runaway risk.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Δ H<sub>rxn</sub> | Enthalpy of reaction | J/mol (or kJ/mol × 1000) |
| C<sub>0</sub> | Limiting-reagent concentration | mol/m³ (= mol/L × 1000) |
| ρ  C<sub>p</sub> | Volumetric heat capacity of the mixture | J/(m³·K) |
| Δ T<sub>ad</sub> | Adiabatic temperature rise | K |

**Indicative severity bands:** Δ T<sub>ad</sub> < 20 K low · 20–50 K moderate ·
50–200 K high · > 200 K very high (assess MTSR and secondary decomposition).

**Reference:** Stoessel, F. (2020). [*Thermal Safety of Chemical Processes: Risk Assessment and Process Design*](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527696918), 2nd ed. Wiley-VCH, Ch. 2–3.
Heat Removal Capacity (Jacket)

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| U | Overall heat-transfer coefficient | W/(m²·K) |
| A | Heat-transfer area (jacket + bottom) | m² |
| Δ T | T<sub>process</sub> - T<sub>coolant</sub> | °C or K |
| Q<sub>cool</sub> | Maximum steady-state heat removal | W |

**Reference:** Incropera, F.P. *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), 6th ed. Wiley.
Jacket Heat-Transfer Area Estimation

| Bottom Dish Type | f<sub>dish</sub> |
|-----------------|------------|
| Flat | 1.00 |
| 2:1 Elliptical | 1.38 |
| Torispherical / DIN | 1.26 |
| Conical | 1 / cos θ (1.41 at 45°) |

**Reference:** DIN 28131 (Jacketed agitated vessels).
Overall Heat-Transfer Coefficient Estimation
Simple Material-Based Estimate (Fallback)

| Wall Material | U range (W/m²·K) |
|--------------|-------------------|
| Glass-lined | 100 – 250 |
| Stainless steel | 200 – 500 |
| Hastelloy | 200 – 450 |
| Carbon steel | 150 – 350 |

**Reference:** Perry, R.H. & Green, D.W. (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), 9th ed. McGraw-Hill, Section 11.
Individual Resistances Approach

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| h<sub>i</sub> | Process-side (internal) heat-transfer coefficient | W/(m²·K) |
| x<sub>w</sub> | Wall thickness | m |
| k<sub>w</sub> | Wall thermal conductivity | W/(m·K) |
| h<sub>o</sub> | Utility-side (jacket) heat-transfer coefficient | W/(m²·K) |
| R<sub>f</sub> | Fouling resistance | m²·K/W |

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 3.
Process-Side Coefficient (Nusselt Correlation)

| Symbol | Description | Typical value |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| C | Correlation constant | 0.36 (radial turbine, baffled) |
| N | Impeller speed | rev/s |
| D<sub>i</sub> | Impeller diameter | m |
| D<sub>T</sub> | Tank diameter | m |
| k<sub>f</sub> | Fluid thermal conductivity | W/(m·K) |
| C<sub>p</sub> | Fluid specific heat capacity | J/(kg·K) |
| μ / μ<sub>w</sub> | Viscosity ratio (bulk / wall) | ≈ 1 for moderate ΔT |

**Reference:** DIN 28131; Sieder, E.N. & Tate, G.E. (1936). Heat transfer and pressure drop of liquids in tubes. [*Ind. Eng. Chem.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/ie50324a027), 28(12), 1429–1435.
Wall Thermal Conductivity

| Material | k<sub>w</sub> (W/(m·K)) |
|----------|-----------------|
| Stainless steel (316/304) | 16 |
| Hastelloy C-276 | 12 |
| Carbon steel | 50 |
| Glass lining | 1.0 |
| Titanium | 22 |
| Inconel | 15 |

For **glass-lined** vessels:

R<sub>wall</sub> = fracx<sub>glass</sub>k<sub>glass</sub> + fracx<sub>steel</sub>k<sub>steel</sub>

**Reference:** Perry & Green (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), Table 11-7.
Jacket-Side Coefficient

| Jacket Type | Typical h<sub>o</sub> (W/(m²·K)) |
|-------------|--------------------------|
| Simple jacket (water/glycol) | 1500 |
| Half-pipe coil | 2500 |
| Dimple jacket | 1200 |

**Reference:** Perry & Green (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), Section 11.
Fouling Resistance

| Condition | R<sub>f</sub> (m²·K/W) |
|-----------|----------------|
| Clean (fresh equipment) | 0.0001 |
| Moderate (pharmaceutical) | 0.0002 |
| Heavy fouling | 0.001 |

Default value: **0.0002 m²·K/W** (moderate pharmaceutical process).

**Reference:** Perry & Green (2019). [*Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0071834087), Table 11-9.
Heat Balance Assessment

| Q<sub>gen</sub> / Q<sub>cool</sub> | Assessment |
|---------------------|------------|
| < 0.25 | Easily manageable |
| 0.25 – 0.50 | Comfortable margin |
| 0.50 – 0.75 | Moderate – monitor closely |
| 0.75 – 1.00 | ⚠️ Tight – limited safety margin |
| > 1.00 | 🔴 Insufficient cooling capacity |
Time to Cool or Heat (Batch)

items.latex: t = \frac{\rho \, V \, C_p}{U \, A} \, \ln \frac{T_{\text{start}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}{T_{\text{end}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}

items.text:
| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| ρ | Fluid density | kg/m³ |
| V | Liquid volume | m³ |
| C<sub>p</sub> | Specific heat capacity | J/(kg·K) |
| U | Overall heat-transfer coefficient | W/(m²·K) |
| A | Heat-transfer area | m² |
| T<sub>start</sub> | Initial batch temperature | °C |
| T<sub>end</sub> | Target batch temperature | °C |
| T<sub>jacket</sub> | Jacket / coolant temperature | °C |

Standard logarithmic solution for a well-mixed batch with constant U, A,
and jacket temperature.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 5.
Terminal Settling Velocity

**Stokes regime** (Re<sub>p</sub> < 0.1): valid for small or slow-settling particles.
φ is the sphericity (shape factor, 0–1).

For intermediate Reynolds numbers (0.1 < Re<sub>p</sub> < 1000) the
**Schiller-Naumann** drag correction is applied iteratively:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| d<sub>p</sub> | Particle diameter (typically D50) | m |
| g | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |
| Δρ | ∣ρ<sub>p</sub> - ρ<sub>L</sub>∣ | kg/m³ |
| μ | Dynamic viscosity | Pa·s |
| φ | Sphericity / shape factor | – |

**Reference:** Clift, R., Grace, J.R. & Weber, M.E. (1978). [*Bubbles, Drops, and Particles*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780121769505), Academic Press; Schiller, L. & Naumann, A. (1935). *Z. Ver. Dtsch. Ing.*, 77, 318–320.
Particle Reynolds Number

Classifies the flow regime around a settling particle.

**Reference:** Clift *et al.* (1978).
Zwietering Just-Suspended Speed

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| S | Zwietering constant (geometry-dependent) | – |
| ν | Kinematic viscosity | m²/s |
| d<sub>p</sub> | Mass-mean particle diameter | m |
| g | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |
| Δρ | ∣ρ<sub>p</sub> - ρ<sub>L</sub>∣ | kg/m³ |
| ρ<sub>L</sub> | Liquid density | kg/m³ |
| X | Solids loading | wt-% |
| D | Impeller diameter | m |

**Typical S values:**

| Impeller / geometry | S |
|-------------------|---|
| PBT (45° down-pumping), D/T ≈ 0.4 | 4.5 – 6.5 |
| Rushton turbine, D/T ≈ 0.33 | 7 – 9 |
| Hydrofoil (A310), D/T ≈ 0.4 | 3 – 5 |

**Reference:** Zwietering, Th.N. (1958). Suspending of solid particles in liquid by agitators. [*Chem. Eng. Sci.*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0009-2509%2858%2985031-9), 8(3–4), 244–253.
Grenville, Mak & Brown (GMB) Just-Suspended Speed

items.latex: N_{js} = z \, Po^{-1/3} \, D^{-2/3} \left(\frac{g\,\Delta\rho}{\rho_L}\right)^{0.5} X_v^{0.154} \, d_p^{0.167} \left(\frac{C}{D}\right)^{0.1}

items.text:
An alternative to Zwietering that uses the **power number** Po and
**impeller clearance ratio** C/D explicitly.

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| z | Geometry constant (impeller-type dependent) | – |
| Po | Power number (N<sub>p</sub>) | – |
| D | Impeller diameter | m |
| g | Gravitational acceleration | m/s² |
| Δρ | ∣ρ<sub>p</sub> - ρ<sub>L</sub>∣ | kg/m³ |
| ρ<sub>L</sub> | Liquid density | kg/m³ |
| X<sub>v</sub> | Volume percent of solids | vol-% |
| d<sub>p</sub> | Particle diameter | m |
| C/D | Impeller clearance / impeller diameter | – |

In addition to the standard **literature correlations** used throughout
Mixing Lab, reactor-specific correlations can be registered from:

- **Experimental** – fitted directly to measured data (e.g. kLa from

These override the literature correlation for a specific parameter when
the corresponding mode is selected on the **Vessel Assessment** or
**Vessel Comparison** pages.

Impeller Power (Agitator Heat Input)

All mechanical energy dissipated by the impeller is ultimately converted to
heat in the fluid. This is added as a heat source in the transient energy balance.

| Symbol | Description | Units |

| P | Impeller power draw | W |
Steady-State Heat Duty

The maximum instantaneous heat removal/addition rate at any point in time.
As the batch temperature approaches the jacket temperature, Δ T and
therefore Q decrease exponentially.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007), Ch. 3.
Instantaneous Cooling / Heating Rate

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Q<sub>jacket</sub> | Heat transfer through jacket (= U A (T<sub>jacket</sub> - T); positive when the jacket heats the batch) | W |
| P<sub>agitator</sub> | Impeller power dissipation (always heats) | W |
| Q<sub>rxn</sub> | Reaction heat (positive = exothermic, heats) | W |
| ρ  V  C<sub>p</sub> | Thermal mass of batch | J/K |
Analytical Batch Time (Log-Mean)

items.latex: t = \frac{\rho \, V \, C_p}{U \, A} \, \ln \frac{T_{\text{start}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}{T_{\text{end}} - T_{\text{jacket}}}

items.text:
Assumes constant U, A, and jacket temperature, with no agitator heat or
reaction heat. This is the standard analytical solution for an
exponentially-decaying driving force.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 5.
Transient Model — Constant Jacket Temperature (Euler Integration)

items.latex: \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{U \, A \,(T_{\text{jacket}} - T) + P_{\text{agitator}} + Q_{\text{rxn}}}{\rho \, V \, C_p}

items.text:
A forward Euler integration of the energy balance at each time step.

**Sign convention:**
- U · A · (T<sub>jacket</sub> - T): positive when jacket is hotter (heating), negative when cooler (cooling)
- P<sub>agitator</sub>: always positive (adds heat to batch)
- Q<sub>rxn</sub>: positive = exothermic (adds heat)

Integration stops when T reaches T<sub>target</sub> or t reaches t<sub>max</sub>.
Transient Model — Variable Jacket Temperature (NTU-Effectiveness)

When the jacket fluid has a finite flow rate, the outlet temperature differs
from the inlet. The NTU-effectiveness method models this:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| NTU | Number of Transfer Units | — |
| ε | Heat exchanger effectiveness | — |
| ṁ<sub>j</sub> | Jacket mass flow rate | kg/s |
| C<sub>p,j</sub> | Jacket fluid specific heat capacity | J/(kg·K) |
| T<sub>j,in</sub> | Jacket inlet temperature (constant) | °C |
| T<sub>j,out</sub> | Jacket outlet temperature (varies) | °C |

At each time step, Q<sub>jacket</sub> is computed using the current batch
temperature and the effectiveness, then the batch temperature is updated
via the same Euler integration as the constant-jacket model.

**Key insight:** Lower jacket flow rates → higher NTU → higher effectiveness
but also higher jacket outlet temperature, which reduces the effective Δ T.

**Reference:** Incropera *et al.* (2007). [*Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*](https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0471457280), Ch. 11 (Heat Exchangers).
